questiontext.text: What is the main purpose of chaos engineering practices, such as randomly terminating servers in a running system?

generalfeedback.text: Chaos engineering deliberately introduces failures, such as terminating servers or whole zones, to prove continuously that automated recovery works and that users do not notice. Stopping a server to find its owner is the scream test, not chaos engineering. Deliberate failures depend on monitoring and alerting rather than replacing them.

answer.text: To cut cloud costs by finding servers that have no remaining users and can be deleted
To identify who owns each server, by waiting to see which team complains after it stops
To show, again and again, that the system recovers from failures without users noticing
To reduce the need for monitoring, since failures introduced on purpose need no alerts

name.text: L4 Q2 Regions and availability zones

questiontext.text: A service must stay available if one data center in a cloud region fails. Which placement meets that requirement?

generalfeedback.text: A region is a geographic location; its availability zones are physically separate data centers located close to each other. Placing instances in different zones lets the service survive the loss of one data center. Extra instances in a single zone share that zone's failure, and moving every instance to a different region is not needed for this goal.

answer.text: Spread instances across availability zones, which are separate data centers in one region
Put the instances in one availability zone, since each zone already spans several regions
Use a different region for each instance, because zones in a region usually share a building
Add instances inside one zone, since extra capacity there gives the same failure protection

questiontext.text: An engineer finds a server that seems unused, has no known owner, and receives almost no traffic. What does a "scream test" involve?

generalfeedback.text: A scream test stops, rather than deletes, seemingly unused infrastructure and waits to see whether anyone complains. Silence suggests the resource is unused; a complaint identifies a dependency or owner. Because the resource is only stopped, it can be brought back. The same approach can also check whether monitoring and alerting notice the outage.

answer.text: Deleting the server and its backups at once, since unused infrastructure only adds cost
Sending a burst of traffic to it to check whether it survives a sudden spike in load
Rebuilding it from code under a new name, so that its owner can be identified later
Stopping the server for a while and waiting to see whether anyone reports a problem

name.text: L4 Q4 Organizing a growing playbook

questiontext.text: A single playbook has grown to several hundred lines. It configures web servers, databases, and batch jobs, and a service's restart handler is defined far from the tasks that notify it. Which reorganization helps most?

generalfeedback.text: A good rule of thumb is to work on code that fits in your head. When a playbook grows to several hundred lines, split it into included task files or roles, separate concerns such as web servers, databases, and batch jobs, and keep things that change for the same reason, such as a service's tasks and its handler, close together. Comments do not reduce the size, one file per task scatters related parts, and per-type copies duplicate code that then diverges.

answer.text: Keep one file so every dependency stays visible, and add comments that link tasks to handlers
Split it into roles or included files that each fit in your head, grouping what changes together
Split it into one file per task so each file stays short, even if handlers end up far from tasks
Copy it into one repository per server type, so each copy can shrink as the copies diverge

name.text: L4 Q5 Testing from a clean state

questiontext.text: A developer tests a provisioning definition by applying each new change to the same long-lived test machine. Every run passes, but the first run on a new machine fails. Which explanation and practice are most useful?

generalfeedback.text: Repeatedly applying changes to one machine accumulates state, so a step that only worked because of earlier leftovers can go unnoticed. Testing regularly from an empty state, as well as on an already provisioned machine, shows the code works on any compatible new machine. Running twice on the same machine or adding retries does not reveal the missing step.

answer.text: The new machine has drifted; recreate it from a snapshot of the test machine and run again
Earlier runs left state that the code needs but never creates; also test it from a clean state
The code is not idempotent; run it twice on the test machine to show it will work anywhere
New machines may be slower to start; add retries and waits, as the code works on the test machine

questiontext.text: Provisioning completes and the application responds. Why is it also worth testing that the machine and its services still work after a restart?

generalfeedback.text: A service can be configured and running yet fail to come back after a reboot or service restart. Testing restarts shows the provisioned setup is valid beyond the first run. Once restarts are known to work, monitoring can restart unresponsive servers automatically. A restart does not replace functional checks, and it does not reset a machine to its image.

answer.text: A restart is the most reliable way to apply configuration, so each run should end with one
A restart resets the machine to its image, which shows whether provisioning is still needed
A clean boot can stand in for functional checks, as a machine that starts usually serves users
Services can work after provisioning yet fail after a reboot; a tested restart can be automated

name.text: L4 Q7 Changes reported on every run

questiontext.text: On every run against an already provisioned server, two tasks report a change to the same directory: one sets its owner to one user, the other to a different user. What is the best diagnosis and fix?

generalfeedback.text: When two tasks set the same resource to different states, each run undoes the other and reports a change, so the definition never converges. Giving the directory one intended state, managed in one place, restores a clean re-run with no changes. Ignoring constant changes hides real problems, and rebuilding or restarting does not remove the conflict in the code.

answer.text: Two tasks manage one resource in conflicting ways; give the directory one intended state
The changes may be harmless if the run succeeds, so they can be ignored once the server works
The server drifts after each run; rebuild it from a fresh image before the next run starts
Add a service restart at the end of the run so the service picks up the owner set last

name.text: L4 Q8 Guardrails for generated code

questiontext.text: A team uses an AI coding assistant to generate infrastructure code. Which approach gives the most dependable evidence that the generated code meets the team's goals?

generalfeedback.text: Acceptance criteria expressed as tests and policies act as guardrails: generated code is revised until it passes them, an approach known as loop engineering. Self-confirmation by the same assistant, a single successful run in one environment, or trust in a stronger model do not show that the code meets the requirements. The team still needs to understand the tests and the code.

answer.text: Ask the same assistant to confirm its output, since it can explain the reasoning behind it
Run the code once in one environment; if it works there, it can usually be trusted elsewhere
Define acceptance tests and policies, and iterate on the code until all of them pass
Use the most capable model available, since its output rarely needs tests or review

name.text: L4 Q9 Changing production without disruption

questiontext.text: A web shop announces multi-hour maintenance windows for each release and avoids changes on Fridays, because losing a production server would be a disaster. The team wants to make routine changes during working hours without users noticing. Which plan fits that goal best?

generalfeedback.text: When servers can be rebuilt from code, are spread across availability zones, and are monitored, losing one is not a disaster. Rehearsing failures, as in chaos engineering, proves that recovery works, and zero-downtime methods such as blue-green deployment keep changes invisible to users. Maintenance windows and Friday rules work around missing automation, manual snapshot restores keep the outage, and chaos without monitoring is reckless.

answer.text: Make servers rebuildable from code, spread them across zones, rehearse failures, and deploy without downtime
Keep the maintenance windows but shorten them, and require two engineers to approve any change that is made on a Friday
Take more frequent snapshots of the production servers, and restore them by hand whenever a release causes an outage
Start terminating random production servers straight away, and add monitoring later if users begin to report failures

name.text: L4 Q10 Acting on an AI code review

questiontext.text: An AI assistant reviewed a playbook it helped write. It reported a private key committed to the repository, a bug that leaves the application stopped after a restart, and a shell command used where a state-aware module now exists. Unasked, it also split the small playbook into many files. Which response is best?

generalfeedback.text: Secrets such as private keys do not belong in version control, even in a private repository. A bug found in review should be fixed together with a test that would have caught it, so it cannot silently return. A module with built-in state management is more reliable than a shell command with a guard. AI suggestions still need review: an unrequested split of a small playbook adds structure without benefit.

answer.text: Accept all of the changes as generated, including the new file layout, because the review found the problems by itself
Make the repository private so the key can stay, fix the bug by hand, and keep the shell command because it already works
Set the findings aside, because the playbook completed without errors and a successful run usually means the code is correct
Remove the key from version control, fix the bug with a test that reproduces it, use the module, and undo the needless split
